claims.target_lexeme: Snolly Goster (1845 frontier tall-talk open compound)
claims.case_section: 2. Cincinnati's Fulton Institute (1845) and Early Univerbation (1846–1853)
claims.short_label: Co-earliest Oct. 9, 1845 printings ('Snolly Goster' < Cincinnati Commercial) antedate OED April 7, 1846 by 5 mos., 29 days
claims.statement: Woodstock, Virginia's Sentinel of the Valley and southern Maryland's Port Tobacco Times independently printed 'a rale self-propelling double-revolving locomotive Snolly Goster' on October 9, 1845—both crediting the Cincinnati Commercial—and Scientific American's December 18, 1845 printing preserved the performance subtitle '(AS SPOKEN AT THE FULTON INSTITUTE.)', advancing OED Online's April 7, 1846 Frankfort Commonwealth baseline by 5 months and 29 days.
claims.rationale: Two geographically separate October 9, 1845 newspaper issues and Scientific American's Fulton Institute header establish late-September/early-October 1845 Cincinnati popular recitation as the source of the ring-tailed-roarer monologue from which OED's abridged 1846 Branch II text descended.

evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: The exact September or early October 1845 issue date of the lost upstream Cincinnati Commercial printing or the name of the Fulton Institute speaker.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: Whether an unmicrofilmed autumn 1845 issue of the Cincinnati Commercial survives in physical Ohio library holdings.

limitations: Jonathan Lighter previously reported the October 9, 1845 Woodstock Sentinel of the Valley printing on ADS-L (Jan. 6, 2024); Port Tobacco Times (Oct. 9, 1845) is newly added co-earliest corroboration.

claims.target_lexeme: Snolly-Goster / snollygoster / snolly-gloster (1846–1853 univerbation and head-noun shift)
claims.case_section: 2. Cincinnati's Fulton Institute (1845) and Early Univerbation (1846–1853)
claims.short_label: Unbroken lowercase solid 'snollygoster' attested Oct. 13, 1846 and freestanding nominal head Jan. 12, 1853
claims.statement: Within twelve months of its open-compound debut, 'Snolly Goster' progressed through hyphenated 'Snolly-Goster' (September 30, 1846) to unbroken solid lowercase 'snollygoster' in Macon's Georgia Telegraph on October 13, 1846 and Michigan's Hillsdale Whig Standard on November 3, 1846, reached San Francisco by April 17, 1847, and shed its preceding noun 'locomotive' to function as an autonomous human nominal head ('a real double revolving snolly-gloster') by January 12, 1853.
claims.rationale: Tracking physical line-end vs. mid-line typesetting across regional reprints demonstrates that solid lowercase univerbation and syntactic emancipation occurred in antebellum print nearly half a century before the 1890s.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Unbroken mid-line solid lowercase 'snollygoster' by October 13, 1846, Pacific Coast diffusion by April 17, 1847, and ellipsis of 'locomotive' leaving the compound as sole predicate noun by January 12, 1853.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Pejorative political specialization prior to Major Beatty's June 1855 Kentucky anti-Know-Nothing order.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: Whether solid 'snollygoster' appeared a few weeks earlier in an unindexed summer 1846 exchange source shared by Georgia and Michigan editors.

limitations: CERT-3200-109 ('Snolly-Goster', Sept. 30, 1846) occurs across a column line break with retained capital 'G', whereas CERT-3200-110 and CERT-3200-111 print solid lowercase 'snollygoster' unbroken within a single line.

evidence.reason: September 30, 1846 Mississippi Democrat (p. 2, col. 2) line-break hyphenated 'Snolly-Goster'.

January 12, 1853 Columbus Tri-Weekly Times and Sentinel (p. 2, cols. 1-2) dropping 'locomotive' ('a real double revolving snolly-gloster').

claims.target_lexeme: Snollygosters / Snolly-goster (1855–1866 political faction and candidate epithet)
claims.case_section: 3. Bridging the Half-Century Chasm: From Kentucky Anti-Know-Nothings (1855) to H. W. J. Ham (1892–1895)
claims.short_label: 1855 KY 'Immortal Snollygosters' and Oct. 25, 1866 candidate slur ('the Snolly-goster') antedate OED 1895 political sense by 29 yrs., 3 days
claims.statement: Partisan political application of snollygoster emerged in June 1855 with Major Beatty's Bath County, Kentucky anti-Know-Nothing burlesque order 'The Immortal Snollygosters', entered Civil War political caricature (1861 'Snolligoster' for Gen. Zollicoffer; 1863 Emmett's Black Brigade; 1864 J. B. Murphy's Snolly-goster Ebenezer mocking 'hungry politicians'), and appeared as a singular personal candidate slur ('R. Cole Foster, the Snolly-goster,' nominee for Kansas State Senate) on October 25, 1866—advancing OED Online's October 28, 1895 political-shyster citation by 29 years and 3 days.
claims.rationale: Primary newspaper and sheet-music scans supply the missing antebellum and Reconstruction links connecting 1840s Ohio-Kentucky tall talk directly to Gilded Age electoral invective.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Partisan anti-Know-Nothing club satire in Kentucky by June 28, 1855, explicit 'hungry politicians' sheet-music satire in 1864, and singular personal candidate invective ('the Snolly-goster') on October 25, 1866.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Col. H. W. J. Ham's specific mock-dictionary gloss ('unquenchable thirst for office' / 'talknophical assumnacy'), which crystallized in 1892–1895.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: Exact June 1855 issue date of the upstream Lexington Kentucky Statesman notice cited by the Canton Weekly Register.

limitations: Merriam-Webster's Wordplay essay noted in prose without quoting a citation that by the 1850s the word referred derogatorily to politicians in the South; CERT-3200-201, CERT-3200-205, and CERT-3200-206 supply the dated primary scans.

October 25, 1866 White Cloud Kansas Chief (p. 2, col. 2) calling State Senate nominee 'R. Cole Foster, the Snolly-goster'.

claims.target_lexeme: snolligoster / snollygoster / super-snolly-gonchus (1873–1953 semantic and rhetorical branches)
claims.case_section: 3. Bridging the Half-Century Chasm: From Kentucky Anti-Know-Nothings (1855) to H. W. J. Ham (1892–1895)
claims.short_label: 1873–1879 'whopper' transfers, Sept. 1892–1895 Col. H. W. J. Ham Georgia Cracker attribution, 1905 Ozark derivative, and Sept. 2, 1952 Truman revival
claims.statement: Between 1873 and 1953, snollygoster branched into an inanimate/zoological 'crusher, whopper' sense (Feb. 26, 1873 Huntingdon Journal; Oct. 4, 1877 Carson City Morning Appeal; Oct. 9, 1879 Forest and Stream) and Ozark intensifier 'super-snolly-gonchus' (1905 Dialect Notes), while Hon. Henry W. J. Ham popularized the anti-Populist political epithet in September–October 1892 speeches and authored the 1895 'monumental, talknophical assumnacy' definition as editor of The Georgia Cracker (refuting his own Jan. 1893 '1848 coinage' yarn), before President Harry S. Truman revived the word at Parkersburg, West Virginia on September 2, 1952.
claims.rationale: Dated primary printings calibrate four secondary milestones simultaneously: pushing the 'outsized thing' sense from 1884 to 1877/1879, 'super-snolly-gonchus' from 1913 to 1905, Ham's campaign usage to September 29, 1892 (identifying him as the anonymous 'Georgia editor' of 1895), and Truman's Parkersburg speech to September 2, 1952.

evidence_boundary.establishes: 1873–1879 'whopper' semantic extension, September–October 1892 live Georgia campaign usage by H. W. J. Ham, attribution of the 1895 definition to Ham's Georgia Cracker, 1905 Ozark 'super-snolly-gonchus', and exact September 2, 1952 date of Truman's Parkersburg speech.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Any genuine Southern dialect currency for Truman's jocular November 1953 'man born out of wedlock' gloss, which contemporary dialect checks failed to corroborate.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: Exact autumn 1895 issue date of the Gainesville Georgia Cracker from which the October 28, 1895 Columbus Evening Dispatch and November 15, 1895 Iowa State Bystander clipped Ham's definition.

limitations: CERT-3200-215 and CERT-3200-216 are post-1930 public records linked externally without hosted R2 scans per the pre-1931 scan rights policy.

evidence.reason: February 26, 1873 Huntingdon Journal (p. 2, col. 2) inanimate editorial blast 'a crusher, a stinger, a snolly-goster'.
October 4, 1877 Carson City Morning Appeal (p. 3, col. 3) outsized-thing sense antedating 1884 by seven years.
October 9, 1879 Forest and Stream ([p. 703], col. 3) 'What a snolligoster!' for a forty-pound Florida redfish.
September 29, 1892 New York Sun (p. 6, col. 3) reporting Hon. H. W. J. Ham's Georgia anti-Populist stump speech.
October 4, 1892 Savannah Morning News (p. 4, col. 1) election-eve editorial correcting OCR 'suollygoster' to ink 'snollygoster'.
October 27, 1892 Henderson Gold Leaf (p. 2, col. 3) printing Ham's 'unquenchable thirst for office' definition four months before Feb. 1893.
November 15, 1895 Iowa State Bystander (p. 2, col. 1) crediting 'monumental, talknophical assumnacy' explicitly to 'Col. Hamm, editor of the Georgia Cracker'.

claims.target_lexeme: Snolly Goster < snoll(y)- + dialectal goster / gauster
claims.case_section: 4. Dialectal Donor Morphology (goster + snoll-) vs. the Snallygaster Inversion
claims.short_label: Coined in Ohio Valley tall talk from transplanted British/Hiberno-English 'goster' ('boisterous bragging') + pejorative 'snoll(y)-'
claims.statement: Snolly Goster (1845) is best explained as an American Ohio Valley tall-talk compound built on transplanted northern British and Hiberno-English dialectal goster / gauster ('boisterous bragging; to boast, bully, domineer', < Middle English galstren, attested 1674–1829 in England, November 16, 1841 in Georgetown, Ohio thirty-five miles upriver from Cincinnati, and 1894 in U.S. Dialect Notes) combined with Scots/Ulster snool ~ snoll ('cringing sneak; to browbeat') or expressive American sn- pejorative prefixation on the Jacksonian quadrisyllabic tall-talk model (absquatulate, catawamptiously, hornswoggle, sockdolager).
claims.rationale: Primary Ohio Valley newspaper proof of standalone 'goster' in congressional-bluster dialogue four years before 'Snolly Goster' anchors the second element geographically, phonologically, and semantically, whereas the first element fits both Scots/Ulster snool ~ snoll and productive Jacksonian comic compounding.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Direct lexical, geographic, semantic, and consonant-skeleton alignment for second element -goster (< dialectal goster / gauster) in the 1841–1845 Cincinnati hinterland alongside a viable Scots-Ulster/expressive snoll(y)- first constituent.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: An explicit metalinguistic gloss by the anonymous 1845 Fulton Institute speaker explaining why 'Snolly' was paired with 'Goster'.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: Whether initial 'Snolly-' directly adapted Scots/Ulster snool ~ snoll or emerged as playful American sn- phonaesthemic prefixation.

limitations: No pre-1845 British dialect dictionary records the full compound *snollygoster, confirming the compound was assembled in North America.

evidence.reason: November 16, 1841 Georgetown, Ohio Democratic Standard (p. 1, col. 5) attesting 'What do you mane by all this goster?' thirty-five miles upriver from Cincinnati.
John Ray (1674, p. 67) earliest English dialect glossary attestation of 'To Goyſter: to be frolick and ramp, to laugh aloud'.
Francis Grose (1787, sig. E4v & *K3r) pairing North Country 'GAUSTER' with 'GOYSTER'.
William Carr (1828, Craven Vol. I, p. 177) 'GAUSTERING, Imperious, boasting'.
Joseph Hunter (1829, Hallamshire Glossary, p. 45) exact o-vocalism 'GOSTER, to boast, to bully, to hector'.
Samuel Bamford (1854, South Lancashire, p. 181) 'Gáwster, to boast. Gáwsterin, swaggering'.
Francis Bazley Lee in Dialect Notes Vol. I, Part VII (1894, p. 331) recording living American 'goster: to domineer. gosterer: one who boasts or brags'.
Joseph Wright, English Dialect Dictionary Vol. II (1900, pp. 579-580) synthesizing British and American 'GAUSTER / goster'.
John Jamieson, Scottish Dictionary Vol. II (1808, sig. 4X2r) documenting 'To SNOOL / snool' ('to subjugate; a cringing sneak').
Joseph Wright, EDD Vol. V (1905, pp. 590, 592) attesting short-vowel 'SNÖLL, SNOLL' alongside 'SNOOL' in Scots, Ulster, and Northern English.
Bartlett (1848, pp. 3, 68) documenting Jacksonian quadrisyllabic tall-talk coinages ('ABSQUATULATE', 'CATAWAMPTIOUSLY').
Farmer (1889, pp. 305, 502) documenting parallel American tall-talk formations ('HORNSWOGGLE', 'SOCDOLAGER, SOCKDOLAGER').
Anchors the October 1845 Cincinnati Fulton Institute origin point in the same Ohio River valley where 'goster' is attested in 1841.

claims.case_section: 4. Dialectal Donor Morphology (goster + snoll-) vs. the Snallygaster Inversion
claims.short_label: Falsifies deriving 1845 'snollygoster' from post-1894/1909 'snallygaster', 1940 '*schnellegeister', or Berlin 'schnieke'
claims.statement: Deriving 1845 snollygoster from Maryland monster snallygaster (< alleged Pennsylvania German *Schnellegeister) or Berlin slang schnieke is chronologically and phonologically falsified: monster/bogeyman uses (1879 'snolligoster', 1890 'snolly-goster men') and unrounded -gaster spellings (Nov. 29, 1894 'The Snollygaster in Pollytics'; July 1903 'The Ticklish Snollygaster') radiated downstream from snollygoster prior to the February 1909 Middletown Valley Register hoax, while 'schnellegeister' first entered print in the August 1940 WPA Maryland Guide and violates mandatory Pennsylvania German st > scht palatalization (geescht / geisht).
claims.rationale: Primary chronological ordering and dialectal sound laws reverse OED Supplement's tentative etymological arrow: Maryland's 1909 Snallygaster borrowed its name from already-established American snollygoster/Snollygaster, and the 1940 WPA guide invented an ungrammatical German folk etymology to explain the cryptid.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Chronological priority of snollygoster (1845) and political/fable Snollygaster (1894, 1903) over the 1909 Middletown Snallygaster hoax and the August 1940 print debut of 'schnellegeister', plus phonological exclusion of Pennsylvania German *-gaster/*-goster and Berlin schnieke.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: That 20th-century speakers never blended or confused snollygoster and snallygaster after 1909.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: Whether an unindexed February–March 1909 Frederick County rural weekly floated an informal 'German spirit' guess prior to the August 1940 WPA Maryland Guide.

limitations: Original February–March 1909 Middletown Valley Register physical issues are held on local Frederick County microfilm rather than open R2 scans; pre-1909 Snollygaster bridges (1894, 1903) and the 1940 WPA Maryland Guide are directly verified.

evidence.reason: October 9, 1879 Forest and Stream ([p. 703], col. 3) showing monster-sized animal 'snolligoster' growing out of tall-talk usage.
February 15, 1890 Judge (p. 313, col. 2, 'AN INDIANA HYMN.') depicting nocturnal 'snolly-goster men' abducting victims through windows nineteen years before 1909.
November 29, 1894 Bellefonte Centre Democrat (p. 8, col. 3) respelling Col. Ham's political lecture as 'The Snollygaster in Pollytics' fourteen years before 1909.
July 1903 Walt McDougall Rambillicus Book (p. 140) fable beast 'The Ticklish Snollygaster' five years and seven months before Feb. 1909.
1910 William T. Cox Fearsome Creatures of the Lumberwoods (p. 15) southern swamp beast 'snoligoster'.
Haldeman (1872, p. 12) establishing mandatory Pennsylvania German st > scht palatalization ('geescht', 'hascht'), ruling out *-goster/*-gaster.
August 1940 WPA Maryland: A Guide to the Old Line State (p. 7; cf. p. 348) marking the print debut of ungrammatical 'schnellegeister'.
Merriam-Webster usage analysis confirming snallygaster appears in print decades later than snollygoster.
Incorporates the zero-hit negative-evidence sweep across 1872–1924 Pennsylvania German and 1880–1899 German slang dictionaries.

claims.case_section: 4. Dialectal Donor Morphology (goster + snoll-) vs. the Snallygaster Inversion
claims.short_label: Zero occurrences of '*schnellegeischt' / '*schnellegeister' in 1872–1924 Pa.-German lexicons and zero 'schnieke' in 1880–1899 German lexicons
claims.statement: Targeted lexical audits across four foundational 1872–1924 Pennsylvania German grammars and dictionaries (Haldeman 1872, Grumbine 1887, Horne 1896, and Lambert's 16,000-entry 1924 dictionary) yield zero occurrences of *schnellegeischt, *schnellegeister, or *snallygaster, and audits of Meyer's Der richtige Berliner (1880) and Kluge's Etymologisches Wörterbuch (1899) yield zero occurrences of Berlin slang schnieke.
claims.rationale: Explicit negative-evidence controls verify that neither Pennsylvania German nor nineteenth-century Berlin urban slang possessed a pre-existing lexicalized donor compound capable of generating 1845 American Snolly Goster.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Complete absence of *schnellegeischt / *schnellegeister across standard 1872–1924 Pennsylvania German reference lexicons and absence of schnieke in 1880–1899 Berlin/German dictionaries.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Absolute impossibility of an unrecorded ad hoc spoken phrase 'schnelle Geeschter' ('fast ghosts'), though such a phrase would still pronounce /ʃt/ rather than /-st-/.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: Unindexed nineteenth-century Pennsylvania German broadsides not incorporated into Lambert (1924).

limitations: Negative corpus bounds cover digitized editions of Haldeman (1872), Grumbine (1887), Horne (1896), Lambert (1924), Meyer (1880), and Kluge (1899).

evidence.reason: Haldeman (1872, p. 12) records 'geescht' without any *schnellegeischt compound.
Horne (1896, p. 157) lists 'găshwind' ('fast, quick') and 'geisht' ('spirit, apparition') with zero *shnelgeisht.
Grumbine (1887, p. xii) documents 'Spook' as the dialect term for ghost/hobgoblin with zero *snallygaster.
Lambert (1924, p. 137, col. 2) lists only three compounds under 'schnell' (schnellkeffer, =schreiwer, =wok) and zero *schnellegeischt.
Meyer (1880, 3rd ed., p. 72, col. 1) jumps directly from 'Schniepel' to 'Schnipsel' with zero 'schnieke'.
Kluge (1899, 6th ed., p. 350, col. 1) treats 'schniegeln' with zero mention of colloquial 'schnieke'.

negative_evidence_bounds.corpus_identity: Internet Archive digitized Pennsylvania German lexicons (Haldeman 1872, Grumbine 1887, Horne 1896, Lambert 1924) and German slang/etymological dictionaries (Meyer 1880, Kluge 1899)
negative_evidence_bounds.search_method: Full-text OCR search combined with manual alphabetical page inspection of the G- and S-ranges on primary scans
negative_evidence_bounds.corpus_coverage: Complete alphabetical word-lists of Haldeman (1872), Grumbine (1887), Horne (1896), Lambert (1924, ~16,000 entries), Meyer (1880), and Kluge (1899)
known_limitations: Ephemeral unindexed rural Pennsylvania German newspaper columns outside Lambert's 1924 lexical compilation are not exhaustively covered.
